_comment: Vignettes, letter a (Expansion 6 C.9): the bride of the dead, the bridge-keeper's toll, the last smith, the tithe-barn fire, the saint's bones, the hanging tree. Each needs particular things in the world (game/story/vignettes.py NEEDS) and has its own meeting (v_...) and scene (scenes.vignettes_a.json).

note: {bride} has promised to wed {dead_name}, who died {dead_cause} {dead_years} ago, and means to keep the promise on the dark of the moon, {due}.
{bride} walks out to the graves at dusk and comes back with her hands cold. She has given her word to the dead, and says she will not take it back.

label: Tell me why you promised him.
What does he ask of you, {bride}?
say: He is not a bad one. He has no one. His people forgot him, nobody says his name, nobody tends his grave. He only wants a day that is his, and someone to stand beside him in it. I could do that. It is not so much.

He says he was to be wed when he died, and the day went by without him, and no one has said his name since. He wants the day kept. Only kept, once. And I said yes, because I could not say no to anyone so alone.
fail_say: It is none of your concern! He is kind to me. Leave it.
You would not understand. Nobody does.

label: He is dead, {bride}. A name said at his grave is enough. Don't give him your life.
Your father will have no daughter at the end of this. Is that what he wants?
say: ...I will go to his grave and say his name. I will tell him I cannot. Perhaps he will understand. Perhaps. I was so afraid he would be alone.
A name said over him, and no more. Yes. I think I could do that, if someone stood with me.
fail_say: You are wrong. He has waited {dead_years}. I will not make him wait more.
Go away. You do not know how cold it is for him.

label: It is her choice. I will not stand in the way.
If she has promised, let her keep it.
say: ...Then the dark of the moon it is. I'll say nothing more. I'll lay a place for her at table anyway.
So be it. I will not drag her from the grave by the hair. But I will be there.

note: {priest_full} knows the grave of {dead_name}, or the place where it should be, and could lay the dead one to rest, with the proper office and a name said aloud.
A grave unvisited for {dead_years} wants the office said over it again. {priest} could do it, if asked, and if paid.
magic_note: The dead one's want is heard, and answered, and the cold goes out of the churchyard. The grave is still, and no one answers from it any longer.

label: Say the office over {dead_first}. His name aloud, and the old words.
Lay {dead_name} to rest, {priest}. I will see it done.
say: I will say his name. I will say it as he asked. I will say it as if he were my own son. If he has any peace left in him, he will have it.
Yes. The office, the name, the bells. It was never done for him as it should have been. It will be done now.
fail_say: The words come, but they do not take. The dead one does not listen. Find what he wants, first.
I tried. He did not hear. Perhaps he wants something more than words.

label: Here is coin for the office, and for a stone with his name on it.
say: A stone, and the name cut deep, and the office said. That will hold, I think.
It will be done before the dark of the moon. Coin for the stone, and the name on it.

line: {dead_name} has a stone now, and his name is said once a year at the dark of the moon. {bride} lays a ribbon on it and then goes home to her father's house.
The office was said and the name spoken, and {bride} stood by {dead_first}'s grave and did not feel cold. {father} cried with his hat in his hands.
{bride} said {dead_first}'s name over the grave and told him she could not. Nothing answered. She still goes out to the graves at dusk, and her father watches from the door.
{bride} stays among the living, and does not forgive it. On the dark of the moon, {father} sits up all night with the door barred.
The dead one is laid and the cold has gone out of the street. {bride} is quiet and does not say what she promised, or what she lost.
The office was said, and nothing answered. {bride} keeps her hand in her sleeve now and will not look at the graves.
{bride} was found at dawn on the grave of {dead_name}, cold, a ribbon wound round her hand and her face quite peaceful. {father} will not speak of you.
The dark of the moon came. In the morning {father} found {bride} lying on the grave, dressed as for a wedding. She was cold. She was smiling.
The dark of the moon came and went. {bride} was found at dawn on the grave of {dead_name}, cold, a ribbon wound about her hand.
No one stopped her. {father} found {bride} on the grave at first light, dressed for a wedding, and did not wake her.

title: The bride of the dead
A wedding on the dark of the moon
The promise to {dead_first}
stakes: {bride}'s life, and the promise she made to {dead_name}
plea: My girl {bride} says she is to be wed. On the dark of the moon, {due}. To {dead_name}. He died {dead_cause}, {dead_years} ago, and his name is still known in {town}. She goes out to the graves at dusk and talks to him. She will not eat. Please. Talk to her. Find out what he wants.

{bride} is my daughter. She promised herself to a dead man, {dead_name}, who died {dead_cause}, {dead_years} ago. She has the ribbon already. The wedding is {due}, on the dark of the moon, and I think she means to go to him. I am an old fool and she does not listen to me. She might listen to you.
first: {bride} has promised to wed the dead {dead_name} on the dark of the moon, {due}. Her father {father} wants her turned from it.
{father} fears {bride} will follow {dead_name}, dead {dead_years}, into his grave on the dark of the moon.
news_wed: In {town}, {bride} was found dead on the grave of {dead_name}, dressed as for a wedding.
{bride} of {town} is dead. They found her on a grave, in a ribbon.

note: {hermit_full} sits at the middle of the bridge over {river} and will let no one pass without answering the riddles of the bridge's own past. The bridge has stood {founded_years}, and the old tale of it runs: {founding}
A beggar's blanket across the planks. Nobody crosses over {river} without answering, or paying, or being put in the water. The carts stand in a line on either bank.

label: Ask your riddle, old one. I'll answer it.
What is it you want to know about the bridge?
say: Who set the first stone, {founded_years} gone? Who stood on the bank and said, here we cross? ...Aye. Aye, that is it. That is what they said. You are the first.
Born {founded_years} back, and never walked. A road over {river} that bears every back. And who raised it? ...Yes. The old words, as they were told. Cross, then. Cross.
fail_say: Wrong. The water is patient and so am I. Come tomorrow.
No. No, no. They never knew either, the fools who tried. Come again.

label: Who are you? Nobody sits on a bridge for nothing.
You know too much of this bridge for a beggar.
say: {hermit} watches the planks and not the water, with a keeper's habit of counting steps. This was the toll-keeper here, the last of the old keepers, put out when the lord stopped paying. {hermit} has sat here ever since, asking, because it is the only thing {hermit} was ever asked to do.

{hermit}'s hands know every board. This is no beggar, this is a keeper. The bridge was {hermit}'s charge once, and after the dismissal the old one came back and sat down, as though no one had said a word.
fail_say: Nobody. A beggar. Go round by the ford, or answer.

label: You kept this bridge, and your father before you. The bridge was never the clan's alone. I know the tale.
say: ...You know the old tale. Not the clan's. The keepers'. Then you have the right of it. Go over. Go over.
The keepers' tale. Nobody has told it back to me in forty years. Cross. And thank you.
fail_say: Close. Not close enough. Come again.

label: Here is the toll, old one. For the carts, for the day.
say: The toll. The toll! Nobody pays it any more. Pass, then, pass. And a copper for the river.
Coin is not an answer, but it opens the road. Pass.

label: Get off the bridge, old one, or I put you in the river.
Move. The carts are standing.
say: Do not...! I have sat here since the summer. The water is cold. The water is...
No, no, no! The river takes what it is given. It will take me!
fail_say: Try it. I have held this bridge in worse weather than you.
Put me in the river and see who comes up out of it.

label: You were the keeper. Come down off the bridge and take the keeper's house again. I will see to it.
say: ...The keeper's house. It still stands? Nobody told me it still stood. I will sit by it, then, and not on the planks. And I will see that everyone over {river} goes by unhindered. I know every one of them.
The keeper's house. You are kind to say it. I will keep the bridge, then. As I should have. I will not stop anyone.
fail_say: Do not mock me. I was a keeper. I am a keeper. I will not leave.

line: {hermit} sits by the keeper's door now and not on the planks, and counts the carts across {river}. The carts go to market again, and {hermit} knows every one.
The old keeper has the keeper's house back. {asker} brings bread, and {hermit} tells over the bridge's story to anyone who stops long enough.
{hermit} lets the carts over now, and asks the old questions of whoever stops. Nobody knows who {hermit} is. {asker} gets the goods to market, and does not look at the blanket as the cart goes by.
The riddles were answered and the bridge is open. {hermit} sits on the blanket and waits for the next to ask, as the old one has always waited.
The toll was paid and the carts went over. {hermit} takes a copper from every one that crosses now, and nobody has the heart to stop {hermit_them}.
{hermit} has a toll again, and a cup for it. The carts cross {river} one by one, paying.
The old one went over the rail and the river took {hermit}. {asker} crosses the bridge now, and does not look down. The water has been quiet since.
The carts cross, and {hermit} is not on the bridge. Someone has laid the blanket in the water. {asker} will not say who.
The carts stood at {river} until the grain spoiled. {asker} could not get to market, and the debts came due.
No one crossed. {asker} sold the cart at a loss, and the old one still sits on the planks, asking.

title: The bridge-keeper's toll
Riddles on the bridge
The old one on the bridge
stakes: {asker}'s carts, and the old one on the bridge over {river}
the bridge over {river}, and the one who guards it
plea: There's an old beggar on the bridge over {river}. Sits right in the middle of the planks, and will not let a cart past without a riddle answered. About the bridge, about how it was built. {founded_years} it's stood. I've missed two markets already. Nobody knows who the old one is. Can you get me across?

The beggar asks about the bridge. Who built it, who set the first stone. I don't know! Nobody knows, it's {founded_years} back. I have a load of grain that will spoil, and the old fool sits there and says no. The reeve won't move him. Perhaps you can. Answer him. Or pay him. Or whatever it takes.
first: An old beggar will not let any cart over the bridge on {river} without an answer to riddles about its past. {asker} cannot get to market.
{asker} cannot cross the bridge on {river}: an old beggar on it asks about the bridge's building, and no one knows.
news_lapse: {asker} of {town} was ruined: the bridge on {river} was held by a beggar, and the harvest rotted.
In {town}, {asker} lost everything at the bridge over {river}.

v_last_smith.name: The last smith of the old way

note: {smith_full} could forge {blade} again, made by {blade_maker} {blade_years} ago of {blade_material}, but not with the iron to be had in {town}. It wants star-iron, and the star-iron lies at {lode}.
{smith} learned the old way from a master who learned it from a master. Nobody after {smith} will know it. There is no iron for it but what lies at {lode}.

label: Tell me how {blade} was made.
What was the old way, {smith}?
say: Folded forty times, and the hammer sung to it, a note to every blow. {blade_maker} sang to the iron as the work went. That is the secret. Not the metal. The song. I know the song. I know it, and nobody will ever ask me for it again.

You hammer it to a rhythm, and quench it in snow-water at dawn, never at night. That is all the secret there ever was. {blade_maker} had it from the one before. I have it from my own master. Nobody comes to learn it now.
fail_say: Ask in a better hour. I'm busy. The fire is going out.
A smith does not hand the craft to any who ask.

label: The blade will be yours, {smith}. You made it once, and you will make it again. I only carry the iron.
say: Mine. Yes. Mine, in the end. I'll hang it where I can see it from the anvil. No one will wield it, no one need. It will be a thing of mine that lasted.
You are kind. The blade will stay in this forge, as the work of the last of the old smiths. It will not be carried off to be broken in some ditch.

label: Forge it of common iron, then. Here is coin. A blade is a blade.
say: Common iron. Common! Well. I am not too proud for coin. It will be a blade. It will not be {blade}. Come at the month's end.
A copy, then, in the iron of {town}. It will hold an edge. Nobody will sing over it.

label: The old way is dead. Let it go. Nobody will thank you for the effort.
Leave it. {blade} is a name and nothing more.
say: ...Dead. You say it. You say it as you say the weather. Then I'll put the hammers away, and the song with them.
Aye. A name. That is all anything is, in the end. I will not trouble you more.

line: {smith} forged {blade} again, at dawn, to the old song, with you at the bellows. It was quenched in snow-water. The blade rang true, and {smith} wept without hiding it. It is yours.
The star-iron went into the fire, and {blade} came out of it, folded forty times, as {blade_maker} made it {blade_years} ago. {smith} pressed it into your hands and would not take payment.
{blade} hangs on the wall of the forge in {town}, made new by {smith}. It was not for you, and {smith} will not hear of it leaving. Pilgrims come to look.
{smith} made {blade} again and keeps it, and the old way with it. {smith} says it is enough to have made it once more. You were paid, and thanked, and shown the door.
{smith} forged the star-iron, and what came out was a blade, but not {blade}. It cuts well. It does not sing. Something was lost in the making, and {smith} knows it.
{blade} was made again, after a fashion. {smith} turned it over in the light and said nothing. It is a good blade, and not the one {blade_maker} made.
{smith} forged a blade of the iron of {town}, in the shape of {blade}. A good blade. Not that one. {smith} does not sing over it, and does not say so.
A copy of {blade} hangs in the forge in {town}. Everyone knows it for what it is. {smith} will not say another word about the old way.
{smith} put the hammers away that evening and shut the forge. The old way dies with {smith}. The song is not sung, and not written down.
The anvil in {town} is cold. {smith} sits in the doorway and hums, over and over, a note to each blow, with nothing to strike.
{smith} died at the anvil with nothing on it. The song of {blade_maker} went into the ground with {smith}, and {blade} lies where it lies.
The forge in {town} went cold. {smith} was found sitting by the dead fire. The old way died with {smith}, and nobody had asked.

title: The last smith
{blade}, made new
The song of the old smith
stakes: the old way of the forge, and {blade}
plea: {blade}. Made by {blade_maker}, {blade_years} ago, of {blade_material}. It {blade_fate}. I could forge it again, I know how, I'm the last that does. But not of the iron I can buy. It wants star-iron. There's a lode of it out at {lode}. Bring it. Bring me star-iron and I will make {blade} again before I die.

I am the last smith of the old way. Nobody after me will know it. I could make {blade} again, as {blade_maker} did {blade_years} ago, if I had the iron for it, star-iron, from {lode}. I'm too old to go. You are not. Bring it, and I will teach the iron to sing again.
first: {smith} will forge {blade} again if given star-iron from {lode}: the last of the old way.
{smith} wants star-iron from {lode} to make {blade} anew, before the old way is lost.
news_lapse: {smith}, smith of {town}, died with the old way of the forge.
The last smith of the old way died in {town}.

note: The tithe barn of {town} burned in the night with the winter's grain in it. {reeve_full} wants someone to answer for it before the first frost.
A black hull where the barn stood, and grain in the ash, half-cooked. {reeve} says it was set. The village has not eaten well since {famine_years} ago, and no one dares guess.

label: Let me look at the ash.
I will sift what is left of the barn.
say: There is too little ash for a full barn. Not half of the grain that should have burned. No sacks, no chaff, no rot. The barn was nearly empty when it caught, and someone made sure it burned so that no one could count.
The heap is thin and the sacks are few. A barn full of the tithe leaves a thick black bed, not this. Somebody carried the grain away before the fire, and the fire was to hide that.
fail_say: Grain, ash, charcoal. It tells you nothing you did not already know.
Everything is black, and there is nothing you can read in it.

label: Where were you the night the barn burned?
You have the look of someone who knows.
say: I only took a little. A sack. A lamp in the dark, and it tipped, and then it was all flame, and I ran. My children have not eaten since three days. I only took a little. I did not mean the barn!
It was me. I went for grain with a lamp, there was nothing to eat in the house, and the straw caught. I couldn't stop it. I ran. Don't tell the reeve. Don't tell anyone.
fail_say: At home, asleep, like everyone. I know nothing.
I was in bed. Ask anyone.

note: {reeve} wants a name to give the watch, and a neck for it, {by_due}.
Someone will hang for the barn unless it is settled otherwise {by_due}.

label: Here is who did it. Take {culprit} to the watch.
It was {culprit}. I will say so before the watch.
say: {culprit_full}. A poor wretch. Well. It will do for the watch.
Then the watch will have {culprit}. The village will sleep easier.

label: It was an accident. Nobody to hang. Share out what the fire spared and let it lie.
Hunger lit that lamp, not malice. Let it go.
say: ...Perhaps. Perhaps. I'll tell the watch it was lightning. The village has no stomach for a hanging, and no grain for a feast.
An accident. Aye. We will call it so, and say no more.
fail_say: The barn was set. Someone must answer. Do not tell me otherwise.
No. The winter is coming and we have nothing. Someone will answer.

label: Here is coin for the lost grain. Let the village buy its bread elsewhere and be done.
say: Coin. Coin will buy grain from the next valley. Yes. That will do, for this winter at least.
Paid, then. I will not look for a neck this year. But there will be a reckoning.

label: The barn was empty before it burned. You sold the grain, {reeve}. I have seen the ash.
say: ...You cannot prove... I only... the winter... it was only a little, at first.
Who told you? Who? I did what anyone does with a hungry year coming. I sold what I could carry.
fail_say: Slander.

line: The watch took {reeve} for the sale, and not {culprit} for the fire. The village shares what grain is left. {culprit} brings you a loaf from the first baking, still warm.
{reeve} sold the winter's grain and burned the barn to hide it. {culprit} is spared. The village will eat thin, but together.
{reeve} is taken by the watch, and the village learns what became of its grain. No one knows yet who set the fire, and the village does not ask.
The reeve is accused, and the barn is nobody's fault, for now. The winter will be hard.
It was lightning, the watch was told. {culprit} keeps quiet and eats what the village gives. {reeve} watches you in the street and does not forget.
No neck, no name. The barn burned of itself. {culprit} thanks you without looking at you.
Coin bought grain from the next valley, and the village winters on it. {reeve} counts every sack twice. No one hangs, and no one says who lit the lamp.
{reeve} has the grain, and the village has an unspoken debt to a stranger. The fire is called an accident.
{culprit} is in the watch-house, and the village is quiet. The grain was never counted. {reeve} sleeps well. The children of {culprit} eat at the temple door.
{culprit} will hang at the thaw. {reeve} stands taller. The winter is long, and the grain that should have fed {town} was not in the ash.
{reeve} named {culprit} before the frost, and {culprit} hanged. The barn was never counted. The winter took more than the fire did.
{culprit} was hanged at the first frost for the barn. The hungry children of {culprit} were fed at the temple door, and not by {reeve}.

title: The tithe-barn fire
Ash where the barn stood
Who burned the winter's grain
stakes: the winter's grain, and the neck of whoever {reeve} names
a burned barn, a hungry village, and a name for the watch
plea: The tithe barn burned three nights ago. All the village's grain, gone, and winter coming. The watch wants a name and I have none. Somebody set it, someone with a grievance, or a lamp. I need the one who did it, {by_due}, before the first frost. Or I have to hang somebody for the look of the thing.

You have seen it. Black from the roof beams down. The grain was in it, the whole winter's tithe, and it's gone. I will not have the village starve and say nothing. I want who set that fire. I must give the watch a name {by_due}. Find me one that is true.
first: The tithe barn of {town} burned with the grain in it; {reeve} wants the one who set it {by_due}.
{reeve} needs to know who burned the barn {by_due}.
news_lapse: {culprit} of {town} was hanged for the burning of the tithe barn.
In {town} the barn burned, a poor soul hanged, and the winter came hard.

note: The bones of {saint} are gone from the reliquary, and the saint's day is upon {town}. A seller of relics came in on the road this week and has not stayed to be thanked.
{thief_full}, who sells holy things from a pack, took a room at the inn the night before the reliquary was found open, and has kept a bag close ever since.

label: Where did you get what you sell, friend?
A relic-seller in town on the saint's eve. That is a coincidence, I think.
say: {thief} answers too quickly and watches the door behind you. The bag clinks when it is set down, and is moved between the feet. {thief} has the bones, or knows who does.
{thief} is a poor liar. The bag is heavy and the sleeve is stained with the dust of old bone. The bones are here, or were, and some have been sold already.
fail_say: I sell what honest pilgrims want. Pins, ribbons, a splinter of a holy tree. Buy or move on.
I have nothing for you. Ask the priest who {priest_they} keeps in {priest_their} house.

label: Give them up, or I will take them from your bag.
The bones. Now. Before the watch is told.
say: Take them! Take them! They are only bones. I was paid for the fetching, and nothing more. I did not know it would be so dear!
Here. Here! Do not hurt me. I only carried.
fail_say: Touch me and I will call the watch myself, and tell them whose bones they find.
You have nothing on me. Nothing. Get away.

label: How much, for the bones of {saint}? Name your price.
say: I asked twice as much at first, and now they are yours. A fair sale. I knew it was an honest face.
For you, then. I did not think the dead were so dear. Here is the bundle.

note: {priest_full} was the last to see the reliquary. The lock was not broken.
No thief forced the lock of the reliquary. The key hangs at {priest}'s belt, and {priest} has not eaten since the day it was found open.

label: The lock was not broken, {priest}. Who had the key?
Tell me the truth of it, {priest}. I will not betray you.
say: ...I sold them. A little to the relic-seller, who came, and promised to bring them back. The roof was failing and the winter was coming. I meant to buy them back at once. I meant it. Forgive me, I meant it.
The roof of the temple fell in the autumn. There was no coin, no tithe, only a seller of holy things with silver. I gave the bones of {saint} to {thief} to carry, and they were never brought back.
fail_say: The key was always at my belt. Someone must have copied it. I do not understand you.
Do not ask me that again. Do not.

label: The people should know what their priest did. I will tell them.
say: Then tell it. Tell it plain. I will not be here to hear it said.
...Yes. Let it be said. I am old. Let them do what they must.

line: The bones of {saint} were back in the reliquary before the bells rang, and {priest} walked at the head of the procession with a face like paper. Nobody asked how. {priest} knows.
On the saint's day the reliquary stood closed and full, and the people sang. You kept the old priest's secret. {priest} lights a candle for you every year.
The bones were carried back through the crowd in a bag, and {thief} was driven from {town} with a split lip. The saint's day went ahead. Nobody asked why the lock was not broken.
{saint} is home. {thief} is gone, minus a tooth, and a story is told that the saint turned the thief out. {priest} does not tell it.
The bones of {saint} are home, and {thief} is richer. Word will get round that the dead can be sold and bought. {priest} does not like to hear it said.
The saint's day was kept, and the reliquary full. {thief} went on down the road with your silver, and somewhere another relic-seller is already counting.
The people were told on the saint's eve, and {priest} was gone by morning. The reliquary stays empty. {town} has a saint's day with no saint in it.
The truth was said in the square, and {priest} left. The bones of {saint} lie wherever {thief} sold them. The people sing anyway, to an empty niche.
The saint's day came with an empty reliquary. The people stood in the rain in front of an open niche, and in the evening they went to {priest}'s house.
{saint}'s day was kept in silence in {town}. The niche was empty. {priest} did not come out of the temple again.

title: The saint's bones
The empty reliquary
The eve of {saint}'s day
stakes: the bones of {saint}, and the peace of {town}
the relics of {saint}, and {priest}'s good name
plea: The reliquary was found open this morning. The bones of {saint}, {saint_years} in the keeping of this temple, gone. The saint's day is {due}. The whole country comes. I cannot show them an empty niche. Find who took them. Find them back. I will pay what I can, which is nothing.

They are gone. The relics of {saint}, who has lain in our care for {saint_years}. Taken in the night, on the eve of the saint's day. The pilgrims come {due}, and if there is nothing in the niche, they will have my head, or worse. I have no one else to ask. Please.
first: The bones of {saint} were stolen from the temple of {town}, and the saint's day is {due}. {priest} begs you find them.
{priest} must show the relics of {saint} {due}, and they are gone.
news_lapse: The saint's day of {saint} passed in {town} with no relics to show.
In {town}, the bones of {saint} were never found.

note: At {scar}, {scar_years} ago, {scar_hanged} were hanged from one tree, and the tree still stands. At midnight the hanged speak, and each wants one thing.
A tree where people were hanged, after {scar}. They hang in the dark yet, the old ones say. At midnight they ask. The old ones have not answered in years.
magic_note: Under the tree, the hanged speak plainly in your mind, one after another, and each one wants something small.

label: I will go to the tree at midnight and listen.
Tell me what they say, when they speak.
say: One wants a name said to a priest: unnamed, hanged, forgotten. One owes a debt that followed to the grave: it must be paid to the one wronged. And one lies under the roots, without a grave, and wants the earth. That is all of it. All any of them wants.
They each want something small, and the want is old. A name said to the priest. A debt settled. Bones laid in holy ground. It is not much, and no one has done it in {scar_years}.
fail_say: You stood under the tree until the cold got in your bones, and heard nothing but wind.
Rope creaks. That is all you hear.

label: I will read what the tree holds. There are ways of listening.
say: The air at the tree is thick with unfinished things. A name unsaid, a debt unpaid, a body unburied. Three wants, and each answered, they say, would let the others rest.
Under the tree the dead are layered like leaves. The wants rise through them: a name, a debt, a grave. Nothing more.
fail_say: The tree is only a tree, in the dark.
You feel a draught and nothing more.

label: {priest}, I have a name for your book. Say it, with the office, for one who died unnamed.
say: A name for the book, after {scar_years}. Yes. I will write it, and say it at the next dawn rite. It is little enough.
Unnamed, and hanged, and forgotten. I will write the name in, and say it aloud. Let them hear it.
fail_say: A name from a tree? You ask me to put a ghost's word in the book of the living. No.

label: Here is the old debt, in coin, for the heirs of the one who was wronged.
say: The old debt. Nobody has asked for it in {scar_years}. It will be paid, for the sake of the one who is hanging there, if for no one else.
Coin to the heirs, and the matter closed. It is long overdue.

label: I will dig under the roots myself, and carry the bones to holy ground.
say: You dug by lamplight, under the roots, with the rope creaking over you. The bones came up like old sticks. They lie in the churchyard now, and no one has dreamt of the tree since.
The roots held the bones as a fist holds a stone. You got them out at dawn. They have a grave.
fail_say: The roots are too thick, the ground too hard. You cannot reach what lies under them tonight.

label: Fell it. Burn it to the roots. A tree like that should not stand.
say: ...Burn it. Yes. Perhaps. Perhaps that will quiet them. I cannot hear them any longer and I have prayed for it.
Fell it, then. If that is how it must be.

line: The name was said, the debt paid, the bones laid in holy ground. At midnight the tree stands silent. {asker} sat under it until dawn and heard only the wind, and wept for it.
{scar} is laid at last. The hanged have what they wanted, and the tree is only a tree, with old rope on one bough. {asker} cut the rope down, and burned it.
The tree burned for three days. The wants of the hanged did not burn. {asker} says they speak from the stump now, and softer, and not to anyone in particular.
The tree is gone, and the field of {scar} is bare. Nobody hears the hanged any longer. {asker} lies awake and listens for them anyway.
The hanged were not answered, or not all of them. {asker} was found under it at dawn, standing, as if called, with a rope's mark on the neck that no rope had made.
{asker} went to the tree alone, at midnight, and did not return. The shutters of {town} close earlier now.

title: The hanging tree
What the hanged ask
Midnight at {scar}
stakes: the hanged of {scar}, and the old one who hears them
a tree, a rope, and what the dead still want
plea: {scar_hanged} were hanged from that tree after {scar}, {scar_years} ago. At midnight they speak. I hear them from my bed, each one with a small want of their own. I am too old to go and answer. I have done nothing for them in all these years. Go and listen. Find what they want. Then do it, and let them rest.

You know the tree at {scar}? The hanged speak at midnight, every one, each asking one thing of the living. I have listened for years from my window and I am a coward. Go and hear them. A name, a debt, a burial: I think that is all they want. Please. Do it, before they ask for something worse.
first: At {scar}, a tree where {scar_hanged} were hanged speaks at midnight. {asker} asks you to go and hear what the dead want.
{asker} hears the hanged of {scar} each night, and cannot answer them.
news_lapse: {asker} of {town} was found dead under the old hanging tree at {scar}.
In {town}, an old one was found under the hanging tree, dead, with a mark on the neck.
